Skin

Melasma creams: how compounded hydroquinone, tranexamic acid and azelaic acid creams work.

Melasma is stubborn, and our year-round Central Florida sun doesn't help. Here's what melasma is, how the prescription creams dermatologists order from compounding pharmacies differ, and what to expect once you start.

Reviewed by Ian Tasman, PharmD, owner and pharmacist · Updated November 25, 2026

What melasma is

Melasma is a common skin condition that causes brown or gray-brown patches, usually on the cheeks, forehead, bridge of the nose, upper lip or chin. The patches are often symmetrical, on both sides of the face. It's much more common in women, and in people with skin that tans easily or with medium to darker skin tones. Melasma isn't contagious and isn't harmful in itself, but it can be frustrating and hard to treat.

Any new, changing or unusual dark spot should be checked by a dermatologist or your doctor, because not every dark patch is melasma.

Why it flares in Florida

  • Sun. Ultraviolet light tells pigment cells to make more pigment. Visible light, the ordinary light we see, can darken melasma too, especially in darker skin tones.
  • Heat. Heat on its own seems to worsen melasma for many people, so a hot car, a kitchen or a summer afternoon outdoors can all play a part.
  • Hormones. Melasma often starts or worsens during pregnancy (it's sometimes called the "mask of pregnancy") or with birth control pills or hormone therapy.

In Central Florida, strong sun and heat are with us most of the year, which is why many people here find melasma comes back quickly after it fades.

How the compounded creams differ

Dermatologists and other prescribers often combine several ingredients that act on different steps of pigment production. A compounding pharmacy can put them together in one cream at the strengths the prescriber chooses. The common building blocks are:

  • Hydroquinone slows pigment production and has been used for decades. Since 2020 it has been available in the US only by prescription. It's usually meant for limited courses with breaks, under a prescriber's guidance.
  • Tretinoin, a retinoid, speeds skin turnover and helps other ingredients work. It can cause dryness and peeling and is generally avoided in pregnancy.
  • A mild steroid, such as hydrocortisone, is sometimes added to calm the irritation the other ingredients can cause. Hydroquinone, tretinoin and a mild steroid together is a well-known "triple combination" approach.
  • Tranexamic acid is a long-standing medicine for bleeding that dermatologists now also apply to the skin, off-label, for melasma.
  • Azelaic acid and kojic acid also reduce pigment. They're often chosen for people who can't tolerate hydroquinone or want a break from it.
  • Niacinamide and vitamin C are common skin care ingredients added to support the main ingredients.

Examples we prepare from a prescription include an azelaic acid and kojic acid cream, an azelaic acid and tranexamic acid cream, both without hydroquinone, and hydroquinone creams at moderate and high strengths.

Why your prescriber picks one over another

Your prescriber weighs how long you've had melasma, what you've already tried, how sensitive your skin is, your skin tone, and whether you're pregnant, breastfeeding or planning a pregnancy. A common pattern is a stronger cream for a set period, then a gentler hydroquinone-free cream to keep results. That choice belongs to your prescriber.

What to expect

  • It takes time. Improvement usually takes at least a couple of months of steady use, and patches fade gradually.
  • Melasma tends to come back, especially after sun or heat, so many people need a longer-term plan.
  • Mild irritation is common at first. Tell your prescriber if it doesn't settle.
Sunscreen is part of the treatment. Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen every day, rain or shine, and reapply when you're outdoors. Tinted sunscreens containing iron oxides also help block visible light. Add a wide-brimmed hat and shade when you can. Without daily sun protection, even the best cream struggles. Stop and call your prescriber for blistering, cracking, severe redness or a blue-black darkening of the skin.

Getting a compounded melasma cream

Compounded creams need a prescription. Your dermatologist or prescriber sends it to us, a pharmacist reviews it, and we call you with the price and when it's ready. Most compounds are ready the same day or within 24 hours. Pick up in Oviedo, or we ship to Florida, Maine and Colorado. You can browse our skin and hair medications to see more.

Common questions

Can I buy hydroquinone cream without a prescription?

Not anymore. Since 2020, hydroquinone products in the US require a prescription. Ask your dermatologist or prescriber whether it's right for you.

Is a hydroquinone-free cream weaker?

Not necessarily weaker, just different. Creams with azelaic acid, kojic acid or tranexamic acid act on pigment in other ways, and prescribers often use them for sensitive skin or for keeping results after a hydroquinone course.

Can I use melasma creams while pregnant?

Talk with your prescriber first. Some ingredients, such as tretinoin, are generally avoided in pregnancy, and your prescriber will choose what's appropriate.

This article is general information and not medical advice. Compounded medications are not FDA-approved and are not commercially manufactured products. Uses described may be off-label. Your prescriber decides what's right for you.
